hints: Focus on which functional group allows addition polymerisation, and which groups are just spectators.
Notice compound G has a $CH_2=C<$ alkene unit, with $C\equiv N$ and $CO_2CH_3$ both attached to the same carbon.
Open the $C=C$ double bond to a $C-C$ single bond in the backbone, keeping both side groups unchanged on one carbon.
walkthrough:
**Spot the polymerisable bond**

Addition polymerisation always opens a $C=C$ double bond. In G, that is $CH_2=C<$. The nitrile, $C\equiv N$, and the ester, $CO_2CH_3$, do not react here.

Monomer key part:
$$CH_2=C(CN)(CO_2CH_3)$$

**Open the double bond**

Break the pi bond of $C=C$ to make two new single bonds to neighbours. The $CH_2$ becomes $-CH_2-$, and the $C(CN)(CO_2CH_3)$ becomes $-C(CN)(CO_2CH_3)-$.

Rule for repeat unit:
$$CH_2=C(X)(Y) \rightarrow -CH_2-C(X)(Y)-$$

**Check the repeat unit**

So the backbone must be all single bonds, with two side groups, $CN$ and $CO_2CH_3$, on the same carbon. That matches only one diagram, with continuation bonds through the two backbone carbons.

options.A: Incorrect. It still shows $CH=C$ with a double bond in the backbone. Addition polymerisation breaks the $C=C$ pi bond to give a saturated $C-C$ backbone, so a double bond must not remain.
options.B: Incorrect. It keeps a $CH=C$ double bond in the backbone and also changes the nitrile $C\equiv N$ into $CH-C=N$. Neither the $C=C$ remains nor does the $C\equiv N$ change in addition polymerisation.
options.C: Correct. Opening $CH_2=C(CN)(CO_2CH_3)$ gives $-CH_2-C(CN)(CO_2CH_3)-$. The backbone is now single bonds only, and both the $C\equiv N$ and $CO_2CH_3$ groups are unchanged on the same carbon.
options.D: Incorrect. It tries to polymerise through the $C\equiv N$ group and rearranges the carbon skeleton. Addition polymerisation occurs at the alkene $C=C$ only, the nitrile and ester are side groups and stay intact.
